content:
Read this project brief and explain, in plain English, how the team should sequence its next month of work. Focus on the most important dependencies and give a practical recommendation rather than repeating the brief.

The town archive occupies a converted school beside the river. Its collection includes engineering drawings, photographs, council minutes, recorded interviews, and a small set of handwritten shipping registers. For years, the staff have managed access with a shared spreadsheet and paper request slips. That arrangement worked when most readers visited in person. It now causes confusion because requests arrive through several channels and the same fragile volume can be promised to two people on the same afternoon. The council has funded a modest improvement project. It expects a useful first release before the winter exhibition, but it has not approved a replacement for every existing system.

Mara, the archivist, wants the project to begin with a clear record of what a reader requested and where each item is located. She is concerned that the technical team will concentrate on scanning because scanned pages are easy to demonstrate. Many requests do not require a digital copy. A researcher may only need confirmation that a drawing exists, permission to inspect a restricted letter, or a reliable appointment. Mara has proposed a single request register that records the item identifier, the reader's purpose, the current decision, the next responsible person, and the promised response date. She does not want sensitive research notes to appear on a public page.

Jon, who manages the building, has discovered that the storage room's humidity sensor reports brief spikes whenever its battery is low. A contractor interpreted those readings as evidence of a failing ventilation system. A temporary second sensor has shown that the room is usually stable, although one shelf beside an exterior wall is noticeably damp after heavy rain. The contractor can inspect the wall next Tuesday. Moving that shelf's boxes would free the area, but the receiving room must first be cleaned and checked for pests. Jon needs an exact list of boxes before arranging staff time; a general instruction to move the vulnerable collection is not sufficient.

The collection catalogue contains roughly twelve thousand entries. Some older records use a year followed by a handwritten sequence number, while newer records use a department prefix. A volunteer previously merged several apparent duplicates, including two photographs that turned out to be different prints with different annotations. The project therefore cannot treat matching titles as proof that records describe the same object. The catalogue export should preserve every original identifier and record any proposed relationship separately. Staff can review uncertain matches gradually. The team agrees that a reversible cross-reference is more valuable than a quick cleanup that destroys the provenance of an entry.

Reader appointments present a separate scheduling problem. The reading room has eight desks, but only two are large enough for unfolded maps. One of those desks must remain near a supervised workstation when restricted drawings are consulted. A calendar showing eight interchangeable places would therefore overstate capacity. Mara suggests describing appointment needs with a small number of explicit attributes: a standard desk, a map desk, a supervised workstation, and assistance from a member of staff. The first version can rely on a staff member to approve bookings. It does not need to solve every possible scheduling conflict automatically, but it must show the relevant constraints before a promise is made.

The digitisation station has a camera, a light stand, and a computer that saves images to a local disk. At the end of each day a volunteer copies the images to a shared folder. There is no reliable record connecting a photograph of a page to the catalogue item and page number. Filenames sometimes contain the volunteer's initials and sometimes contain the date. The team has agreed to introduce a capture sheet with a stable job identifier before changing the image software. Each job should name the source item, expected page range, operator, capture date, and any handling restriction. A small sample should be checked by a second person before the job is marked complete.

The network connection is dependable in the office but unreliable near the digitisation station. Buying a faster internet subscription would not repair this local wireless problem. The technician can install a cable along an existing conduit, but the building manager must confirm that the route does not disturb protected fittings. Until then, the capture station should keep its current local working copy and display whether a job has reached the shared storage. An operator must not confuse a successful local save with a completed backup. The team would prefer an explicit pending state and a retry mechanism to a progress indicator that reaches one hundred percent before the transfer has actually finished.

Access rules are another source of uncertainty. Some documents may be inspected but not reproduced. Others may be reproduced for personal research but not published. A small number contain personal information about living people and require a separate review. The current spreadsheet compresses these distinctions into a single column called restricted. The revised process needs separate decisions for viewing, reproduction, and publication. The project should record who made each decision and the basis for it. It should also allow a later decision to supersede an earlier one without erasing the history. The staff have asked for simple language in the interface because readers often misunderstand legal shorthand.

The council's finance officer is willing to fund replacement storage if the team can explain how much space is required and how recovery will be tested. A large disk alone is not a recovery plan. The archive currently holds one primary copy and one copy in a cupboard in the same building. During a flood, both could be lost together. The team is considering an off-site copy of approved material, with encryption and a documented process for recovering the keys. Before moving the entire collection, it should restore a representative sample into a clean location and verify that catalogue references, image files, and access decisions can still be connected. A failed rehearsal should be treated as useful evidence while the original copies remain available.

There are four people available to the project, but none can work on it full time. Mara can provide two afternoons each week, Jon can provide one morning, the technician can provide three days, and a volunteer coordinator can arrange short sessions with experienced readers. The developer has suggested building a complete reader portal immediately. The coordinator argues for first observing how a small number of real requests move through the archive. Those observations should include an ordinary document request, a map appointment, a request requiring permission, and a request that cannot be fulfilled. Each case should end with a clear explanation to the reader, rather than disappearing into an internal queue.

The winter exhibition creates a useful deadline but also a risk of distraction. The exhibition team wants a public gallery of twenty photographs, whereas the archive's everyday problems concern thousands of requests and catalogue records. Preparing the gallery can serve as a pilot only if it uses the same identifiers, permission checks, capture records, and storage process that ordinary work will use. A separate shortcut for exhibition material might produce an attractive demonstration while leaving the underlying process unchanged. The project sponsor has asked the team to identify which parts of the pilot are reusable and which are temporary presentation work.

At the last meeting, the team drafted a few acceptance checks. A staff member should be able to find the current state of a request without reading an email chain. Two different items with the same title must remain distinct. A map appointment must not be confirmed when the required desk is already occupied. A scanned page must be traceable to its source and capture job. A reader must receive the correct explanation when access is declined. Finally, a person who did not create the backup should be able to restore the pilot material using the written instructions. None of these checks requires a polished public website, but all of them require the team to agree on ownership and terminology.

One unresolved issue is how to handle changes during the pilot. Staff will inevitably discover missing fields and unusual cases. The developer proposes collecting every suggestion in a shared list, classifying whether it blocks a current task or merely makes the interface more convenient. Blocking issues should be reviewed each afternoon; cosmetic requests can wait until the end of the week. The archive should retain the original paper references during this period and avoid deleting the old spreadsheet. At the same time, staff need a single agreed place to record the current request status, otherwise the pilot will create another competing source of truth.

The sponsor will attend a review in four weeks. She wants to see a small working process, evidence from the pilot cases, and a clear account of what remains uncertain. She has not asked the team to promise that the whole collection will be digitised by then. A useful review would show the original request, the decisions made, the appointment or capture work performed, and a successful recovery of the resulting records. The team should also explain which measurements will guide the next investment: delays waiting for permission, time spent finding physical items, failed transfers, correction rates in catalogue links, and staff effort per completed request. The immediate task is to choose a sequence that makes these outcomes possible with the people and time available.

Give a practical four-week sequence, explain the critical dependencies and parallel work, and end with the evidence the sponsor should see at the review.
